analysis.one_liner: Opens federal prison contractors' records to public scrutiny under the Freedom of Information Act.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee: 33 Democrats cosponsored it, no Republican did, and it got no vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Private companies and state or local jails that hold federal prisoners under contract currently keep their records outside the federal Freedom of Information Act, so the public often cannot see what goes on inside them the way it can for federal prisons. The bill would treat records at those contract facilities as federal records, making them subject to the same public-disclosure rules as federal prisons, with the usual exemptions for security and personal privacy. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — journalists, civil-rights groups, families of detainees, and oversight organizations — who want to see medical care records, use-of-force reports, deaths in custody, and staffing levels at privately run facilities holding federal inmates, which today can resist FOIA requests by claiming they are not federal agencies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Journalists, watchdog groups, and detainee families

how_it_helps.text: Makes any record at a private or state/local facility holding federal prisoners a federal agency record for FOIA purposes, subject to the same disclosure rules as federal prisons [S2] [S3].

Bars federal agencies from withholding contract-prison information unless they independently determine disclosure would cause specific harm under an existing FOIA exemption, or the law prohibits disclosure [S3].
Requires compliance with the disclosure rules to be written into every federal prison contract and modification within one year, and orders agencies to issue implementing rules within 180 days [S3].
Explicitly preserves stronger state and local open-records laws rather than preempting them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The private prison industry (companies like CoreCivic and GEO Group) and state or local jails holding federal inmates would bear new record-keeping, search, and disclosure obligations, and would lose the ability to keep contract-prison records outside federal FOIA; federal agencies would take on compliance and rule-writing work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and contract jails

drawbacks.text: The bill covers not only private facilities but any state or local jail holding federal detainees, which pulls thousands of small local governments into the federal FOIA system and creates compliance costs they may not be staffed for [S3].

Forcing private operators to open their records to public inspection could be used in litigation and competitive bids, raising operating costs that could show up in contract prices paid by federal agencies.

Opponents of broad disclosure argue exemptions already protect legitimate interests like security planning and inmate privacy; the bill tightens but does not remove the balance, and it leaves other regulatory oversight of private prisons unchanged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public gains a meaningful transparency tool: today, private prison operators holding tens of thousands of federal inmates can resist FOIA requests because they are not federal agencies, making oversight of medical care, deaths in custody, and use of force harder than for equivalent federal prisons. The costs are real but modest — compliance work for contractors and local jails, some litigation exposure — and the bill preserves standard FOIA exemptions and state open-records laws. On balance the disclosure benefits outweigh the compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in November 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then a subcommittee a year later, it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the bill on November 4, 2021, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S2].
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action followed [S5].
The bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private prison industry and contract jails keep their records outside federal FOIA, and federal agencies are not required to make contractor compliance a material contract term. The public gets no new visibility into privately run federal detention facilities.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security on November 1, 2022, near the end of the Congress, and took no further action on it.

against.name: House Republican caucus
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 33 cosponsors was a Republican, and with Republicans in the majority on the committee after the 2022 elections, the bill had no path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: Companies holding federal inmates under contract (such as CoreCivic and GEO Group) would have lost the ability to shield their records from FOIA, gaining public visibility into deaths in custody, medical care, and use of force. Their interest ran against disclosure that ordinary citizens and journalists sought.

industries.industry: State and local jails holding federal detainees
industries.note: The bill extends the same federal FOIA rules to state and local facilities that contract to hold federal prisoners, adding record-keeping and disclosure duties. Local governments lose the practical opacity they currently enjoy for those federal inmates.
